passage:
I'm Ritu. Last year it felt like everyone in my class had a thing. Gurleen dances. Arun does maths in his head. Tina draws horses. I had nothing. When the teacher asked us to write "My special talent", I wrote "I don't know" and then rubbed it out, because it looked sad.
Then Mummy said, "Nobody your age knows their talent yet. Try things." So I did. Chess club: I lost every game. Choir: I was okay. Then pottery at the summer camp. My first pot collapsed. So did the second. But I loved the cold, wet clay, and I forgot the time.
I'm still not the best at anything. But now when someone asks, I say, "I'm trying pottery," and that feels good.

qa.q: What happened to Ritu's first pot?
qa.a: It collapsed.

qa.q: How did Ritu feel when asked to write a special talent?
qa.a: Insecure and sad, believing Ritu had nothing special at all.

qa.q: What advice helped Ritu, and what came of it?
qa.a: Mummy's advice to try things; Ritu found pottery enjoyable even without being the best at it.

qa.q: What would change if Ritu only valued being the best?
qa.a: Ritu might have quit pottery after the collapsed pots and missed the joy of the cold, wet clay.

grounding: A child who believes they are good at nothing special tries different activities and finds that enjoying them matters more than being the best.

passage:
Summer camp counsellor's note, Day 5
On Monday, when we went round the circle naming something we're good at, Seema whispered, "Nothing," and hid her face in her knees. The others said dancing, cricket, drawing.
I told her that talents often take years to show up, and asked her to try one new thing each day this week. Tuesday, clay: she laughed at her wonky bowl. Wednesday, cricket: bored. Thursday, the nature trail with Ayesha: she found three kinds of beetles and named them all.
Today she ran to me holding a leaf with a caterpillar on it. "Can I be in charge of the bug box?" I said yes. She didn't ask whether she was the best at it. She just looked happy. I will tell her parents about the beetles.

qa.q: How many kinds of beetles did Seema find?
qa.a: Three kinds.

qa.q: What did Seema's "Nothing" and hidden face suggest on Monday?
qa.a: She felt insecure and embarrassed, believing she had no talent.

qa.q: What did the camp counsellor suggest, and why did it help?
qa.a: Trying one new thing each day, which let Seema discover she loves insects without needing to be the best.

qa.q: How might Ayesha have seen Seema on the nature trail?
qa.a: As a keen trail partner, excitedly spotting and naming beetles.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a girl who thinks she is good at nothing trying different things and finding joy in one of them.

passage:
"Jagdish, stay a minute. Did you make this poster?"
"Yes, Sir. Sorry, I know it's just the chart of rivers."
"Just? Look at these letters. The way you've shaped the G and the S. Who taught you lettering?"
"Nobody, Sir. I copy the signboards at the market."
"You have a good eye. Really. Have you heard of calligraphy?"
"Calli... no, Sir."
"It's the art of beautiful writing. There's a club on Saturdays. I think you'd love it."
"Me? I'm not good at art. I got a C in drawing."
"This isn't a C, Jagdish. This is something in you that nobody noticed before."
Jagdish looked at the poster as if it belonged to someone else. "Can I bring more letters to show you?"
"Every Monday," Naveen Sir said. "Keep practising."

qa.q: Where does Jagdish copy letters from?
qa.a: The signboards at the market.

qa.q: How did Jagdish feel when Naveen Sir praised his letters?
qa.a: Surprised and seen; he looked at the poster as if it belonged to someone else.

qa.q: What could Jagdish do next with this encouragement?
qa.a: Keep practising lettering, bring pages every Monday and try the Saturday calligraphy club.

qa.q: How does Naveen Sir see Jagdish's poster?
qa.a: As a sign of a real eye for lettering, not just a school chart.

grounding: A boy whose teacher notices a skill he never saw in himself feels surprised and seen, and keeps practising.

passage:
I'm Sudha. I always thought I was just ordinary: middle marks, middle row. Then one day in Class 5, Salma Ma'am heard me explaining long division to my bench partner using rotis. "Four rotis, three people. How many each, and what's left?"
After class, Ma'am called me over. "Sudha, do you know you explained that better than I did?" I laughed, because I thought she was joking. She wasn't. She asked me to help two younger children in the Friday reading hour.
I was so surprised I couldn't speak. Nobody had ever pointed at something in me and said, "That."
Now every Friday I teach little ones with rotis and marbles. Maybe I'll be a teacher. I'm still practising.

qa.q: What did Sudha use to explain long division?
qa.a: Rotis.

qa.q: How did Sudha feel when Salma Ma'am praised the explanation?
qa.a: Surprised and seen, so surprised that Sudha could not speak.

qa.q: What did Sudha do with the encouragement?
qa.a: Began helping younger children every Friday and kept practising explaining.

qa.q: How does Salma Ma'am see Sudha?
qa.a: As someone with a real gift for explaining, not just an ordinary middle-row student.

grounding: A child whose teacher notices a small skill never seen before feels seen and surprised, and keeps practising it.

passage:
Every morning in the school line in Indore, Parul measured Hemant against the wall with her hand. "Still a chhotu! Did you shrink again?" The others laughed. Hemant laughed along, but the words cut. At home he started standing on his toes in front of the mirror.
On Thursday Parul stuck a note on his back: MOUSE. He found it only at lunch, after half the class had seen.
That evening he couldn't eat. Papa noticed. Hemant pushed the note across the table.
Papa read it and his face went still. "This is unkind, and it says something about her, not about you. Thank you for showing me." He phoned the class teacher that night, and the next day the teacher spoke to Parul and moved Hemant's place in line next to his friend Imran, who never teased anyone.

qa.q: What did the note on Hemant's back say?
qa.a: MOUSE.

qa.q: What did Hemant's laughing along and standing on his toes show?
qa.a: He was hurt and self-conscious about his height, hiding it behind a laugh.

qa.q: What happened after Hemant showed Papa the note?
qa.a: Papa reassured him and phoned the class teacher that night; the next day the teacher spoke to Parul and moved Hemant next to Imran.

qa.q: What does Papa think Parul's note shows?
qa.a: That Parul is being unkind, which says something about her, not about Hemant's worth.

grounding: A boy teased about his height is deeply hurt, tells a trusted adult and is reminded the teasing reflects the teaser, not his worth.

passage:
"Didi, am I ugly?"
Rashmi looked up from her book. "What? Who said that?"
"Mitali. She said I'm so dark I disappear at night. Everyone laughed."
Rashmi put the book down and pulled Bidisha onto the bed. "Bidi, listen. Your skin is lovely. Mitali's words show she's unkind. They don't say anything about you."
"But everyone laughed."
"Some people laugh because they're scared of being next. Did anyone not laugh?"
"...Suhana didn't. She gave me her eraser after."
"Then sit with Suhana. And we're telling Ma right now."
Ma came in from the kitchen, heard it all and knelt beside Bidisha. "Nobody gets to say that to you. Not ever." That evening she wrote to the class teacher, who replied that she would speak to Mitali and the class the next morning.

qa.q: Who did not laugh at Bidisha?
qa.a: Suhana.

qa.q: What does Bidisha's question "Am I ugly?" reveal?
qa.a: She felt deeply hurt and ashamed, and was starting to believe Mitali's cruel words.

qa.q: What steps did Rashmi and Ma take?
qa.a: Rashmi reassured her and suggested sitting with Suhana, then took her to Ma, who wrote to the class teacher that evening.

qa.q: Why might some classmates have laughed along?
qa.a: Rashmi suggests some laugh because they are scared of being teased next.

grounding: A girl teased about her skin colour is hurt, tells her sister and mother, and is reminded that unkind words do not measure her worth.

passage:
Jaya stood in front of the cracked mirror behind the kitchen door and pulled at her frizzy hair. Her teeth stuck out. Her arms were thin as sticks, and her knees were full of scabs. She scowled at the girl in the glass. No wonder nobody chose her for the dance at the village fair.
Her cousin Jatin yelled from outside, "Jaya! Kho-kho team needs you! Nobody can catch Sunita except you!"
She almost said no. Then she ran. In the dusty field she chased, dodged and touched Sunita at the last second, and the team screamed her name.
That night she told Masi about the mirror. Masi listened, then said, "These legs won the game today. Your hair keeps the sun off. Your face laughs the loudest in the village. That's what I see." Jaya felt a little warmer towards the girl in the glass.

qa.q: Whom did Jaya catch in kho-kho?
qa.a: Sunita.

qa.q: How did Jaya feel looking in the cracked mirror?
qa.a: Ashamed and unhappy with how she looked, scowling at her reflection.

qa.q: What helped Jaya feel better about her body?
qa.a: Remembering what it could do, like winning at kho-kho, and talking to Masi, whom she trusts.

qa.q: How does Masi see Jaya?
qa.a: As a girl with strong legs, useful hair and the loudest laugh in the village.

grounding: A girl who dislikes her reflection focuses on what her body can do and talks to a trusted adult about how she feels.

passage:
In the changing room at the Durban pool, Yuki wrapped her towel tight and turned away from the long mirror. Her tummy stuck out, her legs looked short, and everyone else seemed to look like girls in adverts. She wanted to skip swimming for ever.
"Yuki! Did you see?" Lindiwe burst in, dripping. "You swam two lengths without stopping! Coach said you're the strongest kicker in our group!"
Yuki blinked. She had. Her legs had pushed her all the way, and she hadn't once thought about how they looked.
At home she told her mother about the mirror. Her mother sat with her. "Lots of girls your age feel like this. I'm glad you told me. What did your body do today?"
"Two lengths," Yuki said, and smiled a little.

qa.q: How many lengths did Yuki swim without stopping?
qa.a: Two lengths.

qa.q: How did Yuki feel in front of the changing-room mirror?
qa.a: Ashamed and unhappy with her body, wanting to skip swimming for ever.

qa.q: What helped Yuki begin to see her body differently?
qa.a: Lindiwe's news about her strong kicking, and talking with her mother about what her body did.

qa.q: How does Lindiwe see Yuki?
qa.a: As a strong swimmer and the best kicker in the group, not by how she looks.

grounding: A girl who dislikes how she looks focuses on what her body can do and talks to a trusted adult about the feeling.

passage:
The costume room for the school play was noisy and crowded, and there was only one mirror. Minakshi was playing a princess, and she hated what she saw: dark skin, round cheeks, frizzy plait. The princesses in films were always fair, thin and glowing.
"I look nothing like a princess," she muttered.
Her cousin Damini, who was doing everyone's make-up, grabbed her phone. "Watch." She snapped a photo of Minakshi, then tapped a filter. The skin went pale, the cheeks shrank, the eyes grew huge. "That's what the film people do. Plus lights, plus make-up, plus editing."
Minakshi stared. The filtered girl didn't look like her at all. She looked like nobody.
"Delete it," she said. On stage that evening, dark, round-cheeked and loud, she was the best princess the school had seen.

qa.q: What was Minakshi playing in the school play?
qa.a: A princess.

qa.q: How did Minakshi feel in front of the costume-room mirror?
qa.a: Inadequate and unhappy; she hated what she saw because she did not look like the film princesses.

qa.q: What did Damini's filter trick teach Minakshi?
qa.a: That film images are changed by filters, lights, make-up and editing, so they are not real people.

qa.q: How might the audience have seen Minakshi on stage?
qa.a: As a wonderful princess, dark, round-cheeked and confident.

grounding: A girl who feels not good enough next to film images learns they are edited and that real people come in every shape and shade.

passage:
On the flyover near their Chennai flat, a giant billboard showed a film hero with enormous arms and perfect pale skin, holding a cream jar. Every day on the school bus, Jeevan stared at it, then at his own thin brown wrists.
At home he started doing push-ups in secret and scrubbing his face hard with soap.
His older brother Jatin caught him. "What's this?"
Jeevan pointed out of the window towards the billboard.
Jatin laughed, not unkindly, and found a video on his phone: a poster just like it being made, the arms stretched bigger on a computer, the skin painted lighter. "They even edit the hero, Jeevan. He doesn't look like that either."
Then he showed Jeevan their cricket team photo: all shapes, all shades, all grinning. "This is real."
Jeevan stopped scrubbing.

qa.q: What did the billboard hero hold?
qa.a: A cream jar.

qa.q: How did Jeevan feel comparing his wrists to the billboard?
qa.a: Not good enough and ashamed of his thin brown wrists.

qa.q: What did Jatin show that helped Jeevan?
qa.a: A video of a poster being edited and their real cricket team photo with every shape and shade.

qa.q: How does Jatin see the billboard?
qa.a: As an edited image that even the hero does not match, not something to measure yourself against.

grounding: A boy who feels not good enough next to an edited billboard learns images are altered and real people come in every shape and shade.

passage:
On the day Ankita got her new thick glasses, she refused to come out of her room in their Lucknow flat. "I look like an owl," she said through the door.
Papa sat down on the floor outside. "You look like my Ankita. Beautiful, just as you are. With or without glasses."
"You have to say that. You're my father."
"I don't have to say anything," he said. "I say it because it's true."
She didn't believe him. She rolled her eyes so hard it hurt.
But a week later, when a boy called her "four-eyes" at the bus stop, she heard Papa's voice in her head: just as you are. It didn't fix everything. But she stood a little straighter, and that evening she let her little brother Siddharth try on her glasses, laughing when he walked into the door.

qa.q: What did Ankita say she looked like in her new glasses?
qa.a: An owl.

qa.q: Why did Ankita roll her eyes at Papa?
qa.a: She did not believe him and felt embarrassed, thinking he only said it because he is her father.

qa.q: How did Papa's words help later, even though she did not believe them?
qa.a: When a boy called her "four-eyes", she remembered "just as you are" and stood a little straighter.

qa.q: How does Papa see Ankita?
qa.a: As beautiful just as she is, with or without glasses, and he says it because he believes it.

grounding: A girl does not believe her father when he says she is beautiful as she is, but his words take root and steady her later.

passage:
Usha sat on the edge of her daughter's bed. Damini was glaring at the class photo.
"Amma, why is my nose so big?"
"Is it? I think it's exactly the right size for you."
"It's huge. In the class photo it looks like a potato."
"A very beautiful potato," Amma said, and Damini groaned.
"You're my mother. You have to say that."
"I don't have to. I say it because when I look at you, I see you. Your nose, your laugh, your stubborn chin."
"You're just being nice."
"Maybe you don't believe me today. That's all right. I'll keep saying it until one day you do."
Damini pulled the blanket over her head. But under it, she touched her nose, thought of Amma saying "stubborn chin", and smiled a little.

qa.q: What did Damini say her nose looked like in the class photo?
qa.a: A potato.

qa.q: Why does Damini say Amma is just being nice?
qa.a: She does not believe Amma's words, still feeling self-conscious about her nose.

qa.q: What does Usha plan to do even though Damini does not believe her?
qa.a: Keep saying it until one day Damini does.

qa.q: How does Usha see Damini?
qa.a: She sees all of her, her nose, her laugh, her stubborn chin, and loves her as she is.

grounding: A girl does not believe her mother's words that she is loved as she is, yet the words plant a seed.

passage:
Nazia had a pale patch of burn scar on her arm from when the stove flared two years ago. Even in the summer heat she wore full sleeves, and at the village school she kept that arm under the desk.
But after school, by the canal, none of that mattered with Sumit. He just wanted to play marbles.
One afternoon she rolled up her sleeves without thinking, to aim better. She froze when she noticed. Sumit didn't even look. "Your turn, hurry! If you hit the blue one, you win."
She hit it. He groaned dramatically and fell flat in the dust.
Walking home, Nazia realised she had left her sleeves rolled up the whole time. With Sumit she forgot to hide.

qa.q: Where did Nazia and Sumit play marbles?
qa.a: By the canal, after school.

qa.q: How did Nazia feel with Sumit?
qa.a: Relaxed and safe enough to forget to hide her arm.

qa.q: What makes a friend like Sumit so valuable?
qa.a: He does not care how she looks and just enjoys playing, which reminds her that her worth is not in her appearance.

qa.q: How does Sumit see Nazia?
qa.a: As his marbles rival and friend; he did not even look at her scar.

grounding: A girl self-conscious about a scar feels relaxed with a friend who only wants to play, reminding her worth is in who she is.

passage:
After a terrible haircut, Noa's fringe stopped halfway up her forehead, jagged like a saw. On Monday at her school in Copenhagen, two girls whispered and giggled. Noa pulled her woolly hat down to her eyebrows and kept it on all day, even in class.
At break, Emil from next door found her by the bike racks. "Snow fort? The big snow came!"
"My hair's awful," Noa mumbled.
Emil looked at her hat, puzzled. "Okay? The fort needs walls. Are you coming or not?"
They built walls, a tunnel and a snow cat on top. Halfway through, Noa got so hot she yanked off her hat and flung it on the fort. Emil didn't even glance at her hair. He was busy arguing that the cat needed longer ears.
Noa laughed, and realised she had stopped thinking about her fringe.

qa.q: What did Noa and Emil build on top of the fort?
qa.a: A snow cat.

qa.q: How did Noa feel when she flung off her hat?
qa.a: Relaxed and free, forgetting her fringe while playing.

qa.q: What does Noa learn from time with Emil?
qa.a: That a real friend cares about playing together and who she is, not how her hair looks.

qa.q: How does Emil see Noa's worry about her hair?
qa.a: He barely notices it; he is only interested in building the fort with her.

grounding: A girl embarrassed about her looks relaxes with a friend who does not care and only wants to play.

passage:
Baljeet crossed the finish line of the hundred-metre race at the Amritsar school sports day a whole stride ahead. Her legs burned, her lungs burned, and she felt strong enough to lift the whole stadium. She jumped up and down with her medal, laughing.
Behind her, Irawati finished last, red-faced and puffing. A boy in the stands shouted, "Too short to run, Irawati!"
Baljeet stopped jumping. She walked back to Irawati and slung an arm round her. "Did you see her on the balance beam last week?" she shouted back. "Try that, if you're so tall!"
Irawati laughed through her puffing.
That night Baljeet hung her medal on the bedpost. Her body was good at running. Irawati's was good at balancing. Both, she decided, were pretty great.

qa.q: Where did Irawati finish in the race?
qa.a: Last.

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel crossing the finish line?
qa.a: Strong and proud, as if she could lift the whole stadium.

qa.q: How did Baljeet show respect for a different body?
qa.a: She stood up for Irawati and pointed out her skill on the balance beam.

qa.q: How might Irawati have felt when Baljeet put an arm round her?
qa.a: Supported and cheered, laughing even while out of breath.

grounding: A girl proud of her body after winning a race also respects a classmate whose body is good at different things.

passage:
"Pema! I won! I actually won the hill race!"
"I saw! You flew up those steps like a goat."
"My legs feel like jelly and fire at the same time. Is that normal?"
"That's what winning feels like, I think." Pema laughed, still catching her breath. "I came eleventh."
"Eleventh out of forty! On that hill!"
"Everyone near the top was skinny except me."
Zeenat frowned. "So? Who carried the heavy water can all the way up for the whole team?"
"...Me."
"Nobody else could even lift it. Your arms are like a crane."
Pema grinned. "Okay, fine. You've got goat legs, I've got crane arms."
"Together we'd make one great animal," Zeenat said, and they both flopped on the grass, laughing and puffing, proud of every aching bit.

qa.q: What place did Pema come in the hill race?
qa.a: Eleventh out of forty.

qa.q: How did Zeenat feel after winning?
qa.a: Proud and thrilled, with legs like jelly and fire.

qa.q: How did Zeenat help Pema value her own body?
qa.a: By pointing out that Pema's strong arms carried the heavy water can up the hill for the whole team.

qa.q: How did Pema's view of her body change during the talk?
qa.a: From comparing it with the skinny runners to proudly calling her arms crane arms.

grounding: A girl proud of her body after winning a race helps a friend see that a different body has its own strengths.

passage:
Camp counsellor's note, Wednesday evening
Tonight Gurpreet and Sonali were on dish duty. Sonali said she had a stomach ache and left early; I let her go and rest. I was in the store room next door, and Gurpreet didn't know I could see through the hatch.
Half the pots were still greasy. Gurpreet looked at the door, at the pile, and at the clock. The others were already singing around the fire. Nobody would have known if the big pots waited till morning.
He sighed, rolled up his sleeves and scrubbed every one, humming. It took twenty minutes.
When he came out, I didn't say I'd seen. I just asked him to lead the next song. He smiled, the kind of smile you have when you've done something right and nobody clapped.

qa.q: Where were the other campers when Gurpreet was scrubbing?
qa.a: Singing around the fire.

qa.q: What does Gurpreet's smile at the end suggest?
qa.a: Quiet pride and inner steadiness from doing the right thing without anyone clapping.

qa.q: What did the camp counsellor choose to do after watching?
qa.a: They did not mention what they had seen and simply asked him to lead the next song.

qa.q: What would have changed if Gurpreet had left the pots till morning?
qa.a: Nobody would have known, but he would have lost that quiet sense of being someone he can trust.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a boy doing his chore fully when nobody seems to be watching, and the inner steadiness it gives him.

passage:
Tuesday night
Mummy went to Rukmini's parent-teacher meeting and left me alone for an hour. On the dining table: a whole box of Diwali besan laddoos. Rule: one each after dinner. Nobody had counted them. Nobody would know.
I stood there so long my feet went cold. I even opened the lid and smelled them. Then I thought, if I take one now, I'll be a person who sneaks when nobody's looking. And I'd know.
I closed the box. I did my maths instead (ugh).
After dinner Mummy gave everyone one laddoo. Mine tasted better than any laddoo ever. Weird. I feel steady inside, like my feet are on the ground.
Sunaina

qa.q: What was the rule about the laddoos?
qa.a: One each after dinner.

qa.q: How does Sunaina feel after not sneaking a laddoo?
qa.a: Proud, steady and grounded inside, and the laddoo tasted better than ever.

qa.q: What thought helped Sunaina resist?
qa.a: Realising that sneaking would make Sunaina a person who sneaks when nobody's looking, and Sunaina would know.

qa.q: How might Mummy feel if she knew about Sunaina's choice?
qa.a: Proud and more trusting, knowing Sunaina keeps rules even when alone.

grounding: A child left alone with a box of sweets resists taking extra and discovers the inner steadiness of doing right unobserved.

passage:
"Aadhya! Ma'am's left the answer key open on her desk!"
"Don't, Anand."
"Just one peek. Question seven is impossible."
Aadhya's heart thumped. She could see the red ink from her seat.
"I made a rule last week," she whispered. "If the key is ever out, I go and sharpen my pencil at the back. That's it."
"That's so weird."
"It's easier than sitting here fighting with myself." She got up, walked to the dustbin at the back and sharpened a pencil that was already sharp.
Anand hesitated, then turned round in his seat too. "Fine. Question seven is still impossible."
"We'll ask Ma'am after," Aadhya said. When Ma'am came back, she noticed the key, closed it quickly and looked at them both for a second. Nobody said a word.

qa.q: Which question did Anand say was impossible?
qa.a: Question seven.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling when she saw the red ink from her seat?
qa.a: Tempted and nervous; her heart thumped.

qa.q: Why did Aadhya's rule work better than fighting the urge?
qa.a: She had decided in advance to walk to the back, so she did not have to argue with herself in the moment.

qa.q: How might Anand see Aadhya's rule?
qa.a: He found it weird at first, but it helped him turn away too.

grounding: A girl tempted by an open answer key follows a rule she made beforehand and walks away instead of fighting the urge.

passage:
I'm Suraj. On the day of the unit test, Mishra Sir got a phone call and rushed out, leaving the answer key on the front desk, right next to my bench. I could see the question numbers. My heart started racing so fast I could hear it.
That morning on the bus, Gargi and I had joked, "What would you do if you saw the answers?" I'd said, "Turn my paper over and look at the neem tree." It was a joke then. Now it was a plan.
So I did exactly that. I turned my paper over and counted the crows on the neem tree. Seven crows. When Sir came back, he picked up the key, looked at me and nodded.
I got fifteen out of twenty. My own fifteen.

qa.q: How many crows did Suraj count?
qa.a: Seven crows.

qa.q: How did Suraj feel when he saw the answer key?
qa.a: Tempted and anxious; Suraj's heart raced so loudly it could be heard.

qa.q: How did deciding beforehand help Suraj?
qa.a: The morning joke became a ready plan, so Suraj simply turned the paper over instead of fighting the urge.

qa.q: What might Mishra Sir's nod have meant?
qa.a: That he noticed Suraj had not looked and respected it.

grounding: A child tempted by an open answer key follows a plan made beforehand and turns away, keeping the marks honestly earned.
